newsitem.title: USA: U.S. triple execution set for Arkansas.
newsitem.headline: U.S. triple execution set for Arkansas.

text.p: Three convicted killers were scheduled to be put to death in Arkansas on Wednesday night in only the second triple execution since the United States restored the death penalty in 1976.

Arkansas officials said they were confident that last-minute appeals with the Supreme Court would fail and the three men would be executed by lethal injection at one-hour intervals, beginning at 7 p.m. (0100 GMT), at Cummins Unit prison, about 110 miles (177 km) south east of Little Rock.
The only other triple execution carried out since the Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty in 1976 was also in Arkansas, in 1994.

Amnesty International and other rights groups have protested at the planned triple execution and are holding a candlelight vigil outside the governor's mansion in Little Rock to pray and push for a last-minute reprieve.

"That we would kill three people at a time seems especially brutal," said Freddie Nixon, president of the Arkansas Coalition To End The Death Penalty. "It perpetuates violence rather than stops it. We should not as a state be in the business of killing our citizens"

Paul Ruiz, 49, and Earl Denton, 47, were convicted of killing an Arkansas marshal and a park ranger when they were on the run after escaping from prison in 1977. The third man, Kirt Wainwright, 30, was sentenced to death for the 1988 murder of a convenience store worker.
Anti death-penalty activists conceded they had little hope of stalling the execution order.
Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee has repeatedly said he would not commute the death sentences.
"There are some crimes so vicious, so heinous, so contemptuous of life that the only appropriate response is to carry out the death penalty," Huckabee told Reuters this week.
A former Baptist minister, Huckabee said the Bible contained no arguments against the death penalty.

"Who so sheddeth man's blood by man shall his blood be shed," he said, quoting the Bible. "If there was ever an occasion for someone to have argued against the death penalty, i think Jesus could have done so on the cross."

Angela Smith Cunningham, a daughter of the woman murdered by Wainwright, said she would be happy to see him killed. "I want to see him die. I want to watch it. I want him to beg for his life like my mother did."

Wainwright has twice attacked prison guards on death row and was defiant when he appeared before a state board for a clemency hearing last month. The board refused to recommend that the three death sentences should be reduced or delayed.

Ruiz and Denton were first sentenced to death in 1978 but the convictions were later struck down because of pre-trial publicity. They were again given the death sentence at the end of a second trial. Police in Texas and Louisiana said they were implicated in at least seven other murders but none of those cases went to trial.
A state judge on Tuesday rejected arguments by all three inmates that they had insufficient time to prepare for a clemency hearing.
Amnesty International said 56 convicts were put to death in the United States last year, placing it among the top five countries in the world for judicial executions.

"How can we claim to be a civilised society when we continue to repond to violence with even more vicious violence? With this rush to execution, this show of bloodlust, we are shaming ourselves in the eyes of the world," said Ajamu Baraka, Amnesty International's regional director in the South.
